one_liner: The paper introduces a modified dropout technique for LSTM-based RNNs that applies dropout only to non-recurrent connections, significantly reducing overfitting without disrupting long-term memory.
paragraphs: Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), especially those with Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) units, have achieved state-of-the-art results in sequence modeling tasks like language modeling and machine translation. However, standard dropout—a highly effective regularization method for feedforward networks—fails in RNNs because the recurrent connections amplify noise over time, causing instability and hindering learning. This leads practitioners to use smaller models to avoid overfitting, limiting performance potential.

The authors propose a simple yet powerful modification: apply dropout only to the non-recurrent connections (e.g., input-to-hidden and hidden-to-output weights), while leaving recurrent connections untouched. This allows the network to maintain stable memory flow across timesteps, preserving long-term dependencies, while still benefiting from dropout’s ability to prevent co-adaptation of neurons. The method is easy to implement and compatible with standard LSTM architectures.

Experiments across diverse tasks—including language modeling, speech recognition, image captioning, and machine translation—demonstrate that this approach substantially reduces overfitting and improves test performance. The regularized models achieved state-of-the-art results on benchmarks like Penn Treebank and WMT14, outperforming previous regularization methods. The technique enables training much larger LSTMs without overfitting, unlocking greater model capacity and accuracy.
key_takeaways: Standard dropout fails in RNNs due to noise amplification through recurrent connections.
Applying dropout only to non-recurrent connections preserves long-term memory and stabilizes training.
This method significantly improves performance across multiple sequence modeling tasks.
It enables the use of larger, more powerful LSTM models without overfitting.
The approach is simple to implement and widely applicable to other RNN variants.
eli5: Imagine you're playing a game of telephone where each person whispers to the next. If you randomly make some people speak nonsense (like regular dropout), the message gets ruined by the time it reaches the end. But if you only make people mishear the words they hear from outside (not from the person before them), they can still remember the original message well—this is how the new dropout works for memory networks.
prerequisites: Familiarity with Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) architecture
applications: Improving language models for chatbots and virtual assistants
Enhancing speech recognition systems in noisy environments
title: Recurrent Neural Network Regularization
